en: Master Beijian was a man of exceptionally high character and profound realization of the Way. His writings were marvelous, grand, and strikingly refined, much like those of Liu Zhongxuan of Liuzhou.
Indeed, he would certainly have been ranked among the elders of the Confucian scholars had he not transcended the Buddha-dharma.

As for his ability to remain profoundly serene beyond the realm of gain and loss, and to transcend the boundary between life and death, his written words and speech were merely incidental expressions of that state.
He sports in samādhi. Those who disparage him on account of his literary style are surely narrow-minded; those who praise him for his meditative cultivation are likewise shallow.
Beyond both literature and meditation, his wondrousness is ineffable yet observable. Yet you now gather up mere dregs to compose a voluminous work;
will this not provoke a chuckle from within his concentrated state? Nevertheless, the Way cannot be transmitted through words, and yet—
It is not through words that one seeks the Way, yet the publication of this compilation will surely provide assistance to those beyond the need for further learning (*aśaikṣa*).
In the past, while I was serving as the acting governor of the Tiáo and Xià regions, I once reported the Master’s eminence to the Imperial Court,
and he presided over the Dharma assembly at Daochang Monastery.

The Son of Heaven, knowing his name, issued an edict for him to move to Jingci Temple, where he spent the remainder of his life. His elder brother, Huai’an Jizhao, was likewise a great venerable master (zunsu) of the Western Region;
he maintained a relationship of "square friendship" with my late grandfather, the Duke Qinghui.
This was inscribed by Liu Zhen-sun, a man of the northeast, on the first full moon of the second month in the spring of the twelfth year of the Chunyou era.
A single stream can divide the wondrous Xi-quan spring; with a single turn of the fragrant breeze, it flows on through the ages.
Sitting casually atop the summit of South Mountain, even shattering coral is worth its price. Chan Master Beijian used his writings to carry the Way.

At a time when he was still in the prime of his youth, he was already renowned as a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*); high officials befriended him yet stood in awe of him. Some even abandoned their own [pursuits] to follow him.
He visited [me] and articulated his writings; could he have truly understood my "North Ravine" (Beijian)?
Wuchu brought me the words spoken in his room, and I have therefore inscribed this afterword at the Qufang Tower. — Zhi.

Zhu’an takes “simplicity” as his way of being; it is something used by everyone. Only Beijian [Dahui] pointed toward the realm where cleverness and simplicity fail, reviling the willow while calling it a mulberry, and addressing a tortoise as a turtle.
What is called the "orthodox lineage" versus the "distinctive tune," or "direct pointing" versus "indirect explanation"—these are the offerings of this old man.
There must be those who will overturn his testimony. On the full moon of the third month in the Wushen year of Chunyou (1248). Dharma [Master].
Respectfully inscribed by the nephew-grandson Lingyin (Xinyue).
Since the passing of Master Beijian, the hermitage of Zhufeng has produced a successor who rivals the excellence of Zizhi.

Having met the ancestral master Fozhao, his skillful artistry gave way to the emergence of the unadorned; like a tiger with wings, he soared through the vast expanse, his every movement firm and resolute, his every stance upright and majestic.
Yaya! People know one thing, but they do not know two. This "ninefold entanglement" is merely self-exalting one's own ugliness. By examining the sprouts, one distinguishes the field;
how could my words be false? Those who lack the sinews in their eyes—this old fellow is being wronged.

written three days prior to the conclusion of the summer retreat in the Xinhai year of the Chunyou era.

The Abbot drives the mouse into the corner; blowing the chaff, he hits the grain. Turn over directly beneath you—the sword has long since been gone.
The Dharma-seat is traversed by the feet of faith and spoken from the mouth of faith. With a single step one ascends the heights; with the whole body one enters the weeds.
If you know the heart and understand how to support one another, you should skillfully lean the Zen seat over.
I offer this incense:

this single portion of incense is respectfully offered for the present Emperor, to pray for the extension of his sacred longevity without limit—ten thousand years, ten thousand years, ten thousand times ten thousand years! Next, take up [the incense].

Fragrant Clouds: This single offering of incense is respectfully presented for the Meritorious Official, the Provincial Governor, and the officials of the entire prefecture, that they may forever abide in their positions of rank and emolument.

Ascending the hall, the Master raised the cases of the two great masters Sanxing and Xinghua. One, whenever he encountered a person, would come forth; once he had come forth, he did not act for others.
The other, whenever he encountered a person, would not come forth; only when he came forth did he act for others. The Master commented:

"Before he had even left his thatched hut, three-quarters of the territory was already settled. What a pity that the scale of the undertaking was so limited! When Prajñā comes forth, she truly comes forth. Now tell me: [what is this?]
This is being human, not being a person. (After a long silence, he said:

When the auspicious occasion arrives, the festive celebration begins and he ascends the seat. The Dharma follows the practice of the Dharma; the banner of the Dharma is established wherever it may be. That which is empty is the emptiness of emptiness.
Direct perception manifests within the void, encompassing all. It is like the golden-haired one who, upon yawning, enters the Samādhi of Ferocity;

both sentient and insentient beings bow down before the wind. As the sons look on from the side, each increases their own valor and strength. Furthermore, it is like the kalaviṅka bird within its shell;
its spirit and bearing are already so brilliant and sharp that it has already eclipsed all other birds. Thus it is said: "Before leaving Tuṣita, he has already been born as the Golden-Wheel King."
A house with ten thousand chariots has not yet given birth to freedom from worry; [the Buddha], however, has already delivered a multitude as vast as the sands of the Ganges.
Because the Dharma is thus, how could it depend on anything else? Vast and resplendent, it stands far beyond the reach of thought and deliberation.
Only a Buddha and a Buddha know its true nature. All beings among devas and humans receive this power of grace; ultimately, whose grace do they receive?
Power. (After a long silence, he said: "A single breath remains silent, yet it contains all forms; where can the myriad spirits offer thanks for this impartiality? He ascended the hall and said:
"A single thought at the gateway of the face continues without interruption for all time. To go on like this—what bowl would you seek?
Blocking the path with the path, looking at the tower while striking the tower; clinging to the four worlds, peddling Yangzhou from within one's own house."
Ascending the hall, I have no shame before my own heart or the Holy Monk; I do not seek the love of others, yet I am loved by those who hate me.
To forge a blade, one does not use the iron of Bingzhou; who will help me across all quarters to cut through this entanglement?
Ascending the hall at the beginning of the summer retreat: With great perfect enlightenment as my monastery, body and mind dwell in peace within the wisdom of equality.
Drinking the official wine, lying upon the official street—dying right there, buried right there. Originally there is no fixed position;
why use forceful arrangement?
When acting as a donor and ascending the seat, one plants one's feet upon the very first step, like releasing a trigger for a weight of a thousand *jin*;
this is due to your own power, yet you must not fail to examine it. When forgetting the mind at the stage of sudden realization, it is like piercing a target from a hundred paces away;
this is not due to your own power, yet you must not fail to observe it. Examine it...
Examine this: then body and mind are one, and there is nothing else apart from the mind.

As for the ten billion dharma-gates and ten billion names and meanings—encompassing the Guhyavati (Secret Adornment) and transcending the profound mysteries—one must know that within our school of patch-robed monks, there is a distinct style of wind and moon.
They are wielded sideways or inverted; let go and then gathered back; breaking two into three; demanding what is non-existent and holding to what is existent. Yet...
Although it is thus, if one seeks even a hair’s breadth of him, nothing at all can be found. Tell me, what excellence does this patch-robed monk possess?
From of old, no one has recognized his merit in battle; he simply wishes to reassert his epoch-making achievements.
The Buddha took up a skull and asked Jīvaka, "Where was this person reborn? Jīvaka replied, "He was reborn in the heavens.
Again, he struck another skull and asked, "Where was this person reborn? Jīvaka replied, "He was reborn as a human. Again, he struck another skull and asked...
"Where has this man been reborn? Jīvaka was at a loss. The Master said, "Jīvaka is skilled at discerning sounds.
Why was it that on the third occasion he did not know where [the sound] had fallen? Then, on the previous two occasions, he could not have avoided error. "I dare ask the assembly:
Today, these three—the father and his two sons—were not born among devas or humans. Ultimately, where have they gone? Listen to this verse: The Seven Jewels..."
The lotus flowers open in the shape of the character "zi" (子). One flower, one leaf, one pavilion. Waterfowl cry out deep within the flowers;
the flowers bloom where the waterfowl cry.
The Buddha’s Birthday: Ascending the Hall. Paying back a debt: the seed of the Golden Wheel, the sprout of aged sugarcane. Nine dragons overturn snowy waves;
not even a drop of water can be digested.

Three Gates.
A lion stands at the gate; who dares to look upon it? Within the path of benevolence and righteousness, one lets this move pass.
The Abbot has brought about complications where there were none; he seeks victory within inferiority. To set aside his own benefit for the sake of others—does this not go too far?
Is there anyone here who cannot bear it? (He lets out a shout.)
When the ticket has not yet left Prajñā, I intend to strike one gong and sell it to Baoen Temple; neither making it expensive nor making it cheap, how can one deliberate upon it?
(Looking at the assembly, he says: The government has its official decrees, while people follow private agreements.

Seventy years ago at Huangmei, they grasped the robe like dragons contending for a pearl. Why is it that today, the kalpa remains right here? There is no end to their contention, yet there is more than enough room for yielding.
Regarding those who occupy this Dharma seat: first, they receive the imperial decree;
fifth, they stay overnight in the meditation hall. This talk has spread widely, yet the ill repute remains. One must still attain [realization] within the School of the Patriarchs.
There is no such thing. Today, this mountain monk wishes to clear his grievance for him.
This single offering of incense—respectfully for...
May the present Emperor’s sacred life be extended without limit.
Ten thousand years! Ten thousand years! Ten thousand times ten thousand years! Next, he picks up incense and says:

"This single offering of incense is respectfully offered for the sake of the Lord of the Prefecture, the Meritorious Magistrate of the Treasure Edict, together with all the officials of this prefecture, so that they may collectively increase their years of official service. He then picks up more incense.
He said: "This single offering of incense is not worth a single coin; it is priced at the heavens. It possesses nothing extraordinary and refuses to conform to the common.
Having received it from the Elder Fozhao, I now present it for him as it was."
The General Outline (questions and answers not recorded):
From the beginning, I have never understood the forced arrangements [of others]. Casting it to the ground, its golden sound shatters straw sandals.

The True Person of No Rank has no face; what prevents him from carrying water and hauling firewood? Without intent, he acts as a Buddha; with a mouth, he eats the air. He dwells on the mountain according to his lot.

Plowing while at war, they do not weary of the shadow of the whip. The rice-planting horse chases the wind, snapping the tether; the mud-ox roars at the moon. Seizing the fine weather, they roof the houses;
riding the season, they reap the grain. They deliver their tribute to the royal officials with no further concerns; they sing songs of joy and drum upon their bellies.
Together we enjoyed peace and prosperity. Yet, without cause, the winds of karma have once again surged; fixed karma is difficult to evade.
Before Mount Jinzhou, there was no place to take refuge, so I could not help but pitch a firm camp, making it so that even a crow could not fly across.

This was intended for those monks who refuse to be counted among the multitude—those who assist the tyrant in his cruelty, follow evil and deviance, cast aside the fundamental cause, and treat the ancestral community with contempt. However...
Then how shall we venerate the spirit of the late Emperor dwelling in the heavens?
To offer this profound mind to every land within the dust motes—this is what is called repaying the Buddha’s kindness.

It is difficult to escape the ultimate transformation. The Master’s verse says: "Try asking the traveler dwelling deep within the clouds: How could he possibly answer regarding the peace and prosperity?
The pervasive ultimate transformation is impossible to evade; Ten thousand *li* of Yao’s heaven are but a single speck of cloud."
That evening’s informal discourse (the questions and answers are not recorded):

The numinous tortoise drags its tail, yet every step it takes leaves a trace; the misty leopard glistens its fur, yet every pattern it conceals is revealed. To avoid clamor and seek stillness—[is this not already a distraction?]
There has never been a method for this; clamor and stillness are as one. Layer upon layer of locks—thus did the ancients say:

"Today you have reached the groundless mind, yet you are still pursued by that very groundlessness out of the mountains. Lowering the head by a single inch, they enter the marketplace with hands hanging down;
falling eastward and collapsing westward, they shift their position and turn the pivot of the mechanism. Even so, ultimately there is no trace of a Bodhisattva who possesses supernatural powers.
How does one seek it out? (After a long pause, he said: "It is simply that people of this age shield themselves from it. The Master did not conceal even a hair’s breadth from me.
He then cited Chan Master Hongjue of Yunju, who was about to retire from his duties. The abbot of the monastery asked him: "After the Master has departed, what..."

Ren succeeded to the seat at Jueyuntang Hall. Jian received the seal of transmission in secret; taking his ritual implements, he went straight to the abbot’s quarters. The temple master took Jian to mean "selection" (jian) and intended to appoint him as the second seat.
Jian then descended the mountain, whereupon the mountain deity wailed and cried out: "Jian is not 'selection' (jian); it is 'to choose' (jiao)! Jian subsequently left the mountain.
"Bring back my Master! Thereupon, the temple master pursued him as far as Maizhuang and invited him back with full ceremony.
The mountain deity spoke again, saying, "My Master is returning. The Master [Zhaozhou] commented: "The practitioners of the patched robe (monks) are磊磊落落 (lofty and unencumbered);
they are so wondrous that even Heaven and Earth do not know them—how could ghosts and spirits know them? According to Baen’s perspective, this would simply be a case of the deity hating him."
The ghosts detest it. Yet, one has not even attained half of it.
When the *vinaya-dhara* (Venerable) ascends the hall, before the *ghanṭī* has even sounded, it is already most pitiable.
After the ten strikes have finished, within the sphere of each person, there has never been a shift of even a single hair’s breadth. Why, then, is the final stroke not [the same]?
[The Master] said, "Know where you have fallen" (he struck the meditation seat with his staff and descended).
Entering the hall, he said: "Whether coming from the south or the north, whether ordinary or holy, when meeting a feast one eats;

when night comes one sleeps. To call this 'accomplished' is, on the contrary, to make a deliberate effort. Baoyuan [Baizhang] was limping and dragging along—hundredfold ugly and thousandfold clumsy. Let us just pass the time like this."
(After a long pause, he said: "It is easy to distinguish dragons from snakes; it is difficult to deceive a patch-robed monk. Entering the hall:
withered wood and cold ashes, a copper cliff and an iron wall. Spring arrives without a trace; spring departs without a mark.
Peach blossoms are red, apricot blossoms are white—a scene of total disorder before those with clear eyes."
Ascending the hall: At the very beginning, within hearing, one enters the stream and forgets the object; the path is perfectly opened and cut off. Dust covers the face;
the cave gate has no lock or key—worldly guests have never come.
Xie Chongshou ascended the hall for the first time. Puhua twice kicked over the rice table; Muzhou three times spoiled the Zen students.
At that time they let them pass, yet to this day they remain unresolved cases. Why did Baoyuan further employ such a fellow? A cart must be pushed sideways;
justice must be rendered even when the principle is crooked.
Ascending the hall, [the Master said]: "The Yellow-Faced Gautama used this dharma so difficult to believe to cast everyone into a single net at once.

Why, then, did five hundred bhikṣus on the occasion of the Lotus Sutra assembly sweep their sleeves and depart from Mount Ling? Although Bao'en [the Master] originally had not a single dharma to give to others, it was nonetheless easy to believe.
This allows all of you to advance with excellence and retreat with excellence; it does not merely serve as ice between you and Gautama."
Charcoal. It is said: "If for three years one does not alter the way of one's father, one may be called filial.
Ascending the hall, he said: "The ancient masters said: 'If you attain realization beneath the first phrase, you may serve as a teacher to the Buddhas and Patriarchs.

If you attain realization beneath the second phrase, you may serve as a teacher to humans and devas. If you attain realization beneath the third phrase, you will not even be able to save yourself. He then gave his report.
"Ongao. The first phrase clarifies that one has attained [realization], yet cannot yet save oneself.
He ascended the hall and said: "Studying the Way is like drilling for fire; when you encounter smoke, do not stop. Only when the golden star appears will you have reached home at last.
Baoyuan, however, says it is not so: studying the Way is like drilling for fire; when you encounter smoke, do not stop. Only when the golden..."
The stars appear; Cao’s gate takes Zhengzhou.

On the occasion of the Great Memorial Service for Emperor Huizong, he ascended the hall and said: "The Dragon has departed from Dinghu and we know not when he shall return; I look afar at the Pure Capital, where tigers and leopards roam in leisure.
I wish to borrow the fierce wind to pay court at the Purple Palace; The gates of the Nine Heavens, the Changhe, stand wide open."
Ascending the hall on the Lantern Festival: Before King Wei-yin, everyone was called a king or a lord; their influence spread everywhere, reaching even the most remote branches of the tradition.
There is a dharma-gate called the "Inexhaustible Lamp": where there is light, all are illuminated, and that light never comes to an end.
(He strikes the meditation staff once and says: "On a long night and a distant road, do not carry a torch; let us all extinguish it together and walk in the dark."
Ascending the hall: a rushing torrent that passes the blade, a swift flame that outruns the wind. At the gate of Bao’en, this is not the primary meaning.
Even if you manage to pass through this, you still fall into the secondary. Disciples, do I hide anything from you? I hide nothing from you.
Ascending the hall, [the Master said]: "For twenty years, Yunyan was at Yaoshan, clarifying only this matter: 'The clear pool does not permit the azure dragon to coil.
Zhaozhou, apart from the two times for rice gruel and meals, did not allow his mind to be distracted: 'How has the rabbit ever left its burrow?'"
He cast an iron inkstone, intending to grind it until it was worn through; he returns to him the very bones of ten-thousand-mile fame and achievement.

On the Winter Solstice, he ascends the hall: "The movement of the sun's course shifts; the sun reaches its southern limit at the longest day. Receiving blessings in accordance with the season. Look at the tower striking the tower!
The myriad yin forces have been completely stripped away; it is nothing but a scene of sorrow. Entering the hall:
It has only just been the winter solstice, and ten days have already passed. Look and see—before long, the thirtieth day of the twelfth month will be right before our eyes.
Bao’en is not scratching himself in anticipation of an itch; yet tell me, you people here, on that thirtieth day of the twelfth month, what will you do?
Furthermore, how do you bring this to a final resolution?
Master Xie Zhuang ascended the hall, thrust in his spade, and stood with hands folded. "Before the donkey, behind the horse; plowing fields for a bowl of rice. Xu Liu carries a single plank;
opening up a field to preach the Great Meaning. Both sides are left in mutual neglect. Having cleared a patch of fallow land, he plants emptiness as soon as his hand touches it.

Flowers. Such is the brief summary; it is sufficient for one to behold the scenery. However, as for moving mountains, filling the seas, seizing food, and driving away those who plow—if these are required, they must first be returned to my Gate of Repaying Kindness.
But tell me, what excellence does Repaying Kindness possess? (He gives a shout.)
On the eighth day of the twelfth lunar month, he ascended the hall.
He raised the following case: Emperor Xiaozong asked Fozhao, "In the six years that Śākyamuni Buddha spent in the mountains, what did he accomplish?
Fozhao replied, "I thought Your Majesty had forgotten. The Master offered this verse: "Six years of diligent toil—what was it all for? [He]..."
I ask the King: do you remember? Though one may know it directly, it is difficult to evade; in the end, one cannot be hoodwinked. Ascending the hall, he said:
"Three times I went to Touzi; within the Han-yuan Hall. Nine times I ascended Dongshan, seeking further Chang'an.
Since the night snows engulfed Aoshan, every time I reflect upon it, I feel a chill."
Ascending the hall on the Lantern Festival: Two thousand years ago, at the assembly on Vulture Peak, under the clear blue sky and bright sun, Old Śākyamuni spoke for no reason:
"I saw the Buddha Dīpaṃkara; his original radiance was such as this. *Aha!* Even a semblance was like this.
How much more so when it is truly so?
Ascending the hall, he said: "The destitute are parched; the starving clamor. On the ancient shore the wind is high; in the jade pitcher, spring dawns. To go forth just like this—"
It cannot avoid being partial and withered. The talk has fallen. *Sulu sulu*.
Entering the hall for the Buddha-bath ceremony: Two thousand years ago, when the summer heat reached its peak, what kind of old woman gave birth to such a child?
The nine dragons overturn the waters; the nine rivers pour forth in cleansing. Even when it reaches the year of the donkey, there is only peace.
Entering the hall: It has been ten days since the summer retreat began. What of the water buffalo? If you say, "Once it has entered the grass," [then you have understood].
Dragged by the nose, one cannot avoid wounding the blade or injuring the hand. Otherwise, east of the stream, otherwise west of the stream;
they think only of water and grass, knowing nothing else. Neither person nor ox is seen—this is precisely when the moon is bright.

Ascending the hall, [the Master] said: "The teachings state: 'Wearing a patched robe in seclusion, falsely claiming to be an *āraṇyaka* (forest-dweller), they deceive the people of the world, while claiming themselves to be practicing the true Way.
You all have been thoroughly deceived! It would be well to drag them back and give them a severe beating.
If there were no such person, Bao'en would lose his advantage today."
Ascending the hall, he said: "To realize the One, all things are finished. A monk who has settled the matter does not recognize a single character.
Even if you are thus, it is not yet called the 'Full Exertion. Where the power of Yu did not reach, the sound of the river flows toward the west."
Ascending the hall, [the Master] said: "Today the midsummer season has ended. As for the ultimate matter, what is it? A single pivot in the midst of the sun;

a single step turning the body—encountering the source on both left and right, there is no turning back or evasion. For one who is naturally a cowherd, when have the horns and head ever been revealed?"
Master Xie Jianshou ascends the hall: The ancestral fields of a thousand years— The myriad treasures are nearly ripe, gather them early.
The bottomless bowl opens its mouth and laughs; Sages and ordinary folk alike are satiated with deep snoring.
Ascending the hall on the auspicious occasion of the Emperor’s Birthday: The One Above Heaven, the Sage among Sages—beyond the reach of praise and the limits of description.
The four seas and nine provinces are all sealed by a single seal. (He strikes the meditation staff once and says: To manifest again for the sake of aligning with the Correct.

Ascending the hall at the opening of the furnace: Today we open the furnace. At Baoen Monastery, we follow the established custom; the fire tongs and incense spoons each have their prescribed regulations.

If one waits for the beans to pop before seeking cold ashes, one cannot avoid mutual procrastination. To recognize the color of the fire and discern the intent of the wind—even to "bend the chimney and move the firewood" beforehand—already falls into the secondary.

When Mingyin established Lian’an Temple, he ascended the hall and said: "If we discuss this matter, it is like two armies facing each other in a circular formation, with banners and drums within sight of one another.

Coming is like a crashing thunderclap; departing is like a swift flash of lightning. If one were to always constrain them according to the methods of Sun Wu, it would be much like tethering a Han-lu hound and demanding that it catch its prey.

One must instead transcend the lines and rules, acting with the hand as it moves through space, finding the marvelous beyond the conventional, and contending for victory within the midst of inferiority."

If one should encounter a person with clear eyes, it would not satisfy them for even a single laugh. (After a long pause, he says: "From of old, no one has recognized the merit of his sweating horses in battle;
why need one again discuss his epoch-making achievements?"

Ascending the hall, he said: "The entire Tripitaka is, in its entirety, the teaching of Mara. The sun may grow cold, and the moon may grow hot; that which is false is easy to eliminate, but that which is true is difficult to extinguish."
Ascending the hall amidst the snow: Amidst the chaotic mountains, the snow-clad peaks rise jade-like and lofty; The gate of the myriad practices stands open wide like the eight characters.
Regretful that Sudhana has returned home, In this vast silence, not a single person is seen to come.
Ascending the hall on the eighth day of the twelfth lunar month. (Suddenly brandishing the staff, he said: "If you say the Tathāgata attained enlightenment today, you slander the Buddha.
If you say the Tathāgata did not attain enlightenment today, you also slander the Buddha. Not falling into either of these two paths, I cut off the entanglements:
the distant mountains stretch on and on, layers upon layers of boundless azure."
Ascending the hall, [the Master] raised the following case: Mazu, Xitang, Baizhang, and Nanquan were gazing at the moon. Mazu asked, "At this very moment, what is it?
Xitang said, "It is precisely the time for making offerings. Baizhang said, "It is precisely the time for practicing cultivation. Nanquan shook out his sleeves and walked away.
Mazu remarked, "The sutras have entered the canon and Chan has returned to the sea; only Puyan alone transcends the mundane world."
The Master said: "In one sense, they are all merely playing with the 'seal of the winter melon. Master Ma was slightly better, yet if you examine it closely, he still lacked full awakening.
Baolin said: "Chan has returned to the sea and the sutras have entered the canon; I only wish that Nanquan’s [wisdom] could not be picked up even with a spoon."

Ascending the hall on the anniversary of the Great Memorial of Emperor Huizong: The King of Righteousness and Clarity is an ancient Buddha; though long since entered into extinction, he is ever manifest before us.
He benefits sentient beings like dust motes and grains of sand, and his preaching of the Dharma is like clouds and rain.
Transcending the hundred negations and departing from the four propositions—what, ultimately, are these words and phrases? (Looking at the assembly, he says: Stop your ears and listen clearly!

[The Master] took [the staff] and ascended the hall. He raised the case of Xuefeng addressing the assembly: "The entire great earth is the gate of liberation. Why is it that, though he takes one by the hand, he cannot pull one in?
The Master said, "Xuefeng spoke thus; tell me, who is standing outside the gate?"

Three Gates.
This is the gateway through which Avalokiteśvara enters the principle. As the flower-dragon bell roars at the moon, the empty resonance sinks into autumn.
Having shattered the profound barrier, one follows the current and then re-enters the current.

The one coming from the south is carried on the bottom; the one coming from the north is carried on the top. The moon is bright and the wind is clear; Lake Tai has no lid. (This is the extraction of the essential principles.)
There has never been one who moves long distances without stopping; thus it is permissible to act in this way. There has never been one who remains stationary for long without moving;

thus it is also permissible not to act in this way. Where one seeks to benefit, there is nothing to be benefited; where one seeks to act, there is nothing to be done. Thus it is permissible both to act in this way and not to act in this way.
"You ought to take up the oars; do not dwell here for long. Whether you act thus or not, neither is permitted. And who am I to govern whether you succeed or fail?
For ten years I kept my hands in my sleeves, sharing seats with fishermen and woodcutters. One day I left the mountains, yet the mountain spirits forced me back to my carriage.
Now, with no new realization ahead and having lost my former dwelling, how can you find a way to settle this? (Liang)
Jiuyun said: "Upside-down, he takes up a single holeless flute; he blows with the wind and blows against the wind. He then raised the case again:
A monk asked an ancient worthy, "Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva holds a rosary in his hand—what Buddha does he recite?

The worthy replied, "He recites Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva. The monk said, "I do not understand. The worthy said, "Seeking from others is not as good as seeking within oneself. The Master commented on this.
The Master said: "Both the Great and the Small Avalokiteśvaras fundamentally do not recognize their own selves.
That evening, during the small *sǎn* (informal discourse), he raised the case of Master Baiyang Shun, who questioned Master Ying’an:
"Who is it that does not take the myriad dharmas as companions? Ān replied: "Naked, one goes to the latrine. The Master commented: "Tonight, there is someone who acts like this..."
Do not ask such things; simply say to him: "He who does not take the myriad dharmas as his companion.
When the administrative heads and chief officers take the high seat to give a discourse, if one discusses this matter, it is like two boats meeting in a storm;
it requires a coordination like that of the left and right hands. To be flustered and hurried, or to chatter and babble—this is my enemy, a single stroke of deviation.
Ascending the hall: The destitute are stewed; the hungry are fried. The child of the eastern house cries; the wife of the western house laughs.
Secretly scribbling upon the bowels of sorrow, she skillfully expounds the essentials of the Dharma. How excellent is Avalokiteśvara! His disheveled appearance is no small matter either.
Ascending the hall on the Lantern Festival: the pipes have finished their melodies, the drumheads are worn through; the night is deep and still, the oil in the lamp bowls is spent.
A single ray of divine light illuminates ten thousand realms of tranquility.
Ascending the hall, [the Master said]: "A clever monk is ten times as sharp and poised.

To linger here like one guarding a stump, or to wait for a rabbit over there—last night Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra gave rise to views of Buddha and views of Dharma, so they were banished to the Iron Ring Mountains. Old Teacher Wáng led them out himself."

Jingshan’s Four Paths: Formerly, when ascending the hall, he said: "One person has mastery of the principle (*zongtong*); their illness lies within. One person has mastery of the teachings (*shuotong*);
their illness lies without. One person has mastery of both principle and teachings; their illness lies in seeing and hearing. One person does not understand things as they encounter them;
they fall eastward and stumble westward. Now tell me, who is the one who does not understand? (He threw down his staff and descended from the seat.)
Ascending the hall, the Master raised the following case: Shilin asked Páng Jūshī, “I have a question to ask:
do you not begrudge the expenditure of words? The Layman said, “Please go ahead and ask. Shilin said, “It turns out you do begrudge the expenditure of words.
The Layman said, “This very inquiry has unconsciously fallen into his trap. Shilin covered his ears and departed. The Layman said, “A true master! A true master! The Master commented: “As soon as...”
Born, they were immediately swept away; one could not even secure half. Lost in the eastern corner, the setting sun at the mulberry and elm trees is already too late.
As for what the Layman calls "a master, a master"—tell me, does Shilin accept this?

Ascending the hall, the Master raised the case of Zhenjing, who said: "Do not take 'nothingness' as the understanding; nothingness confounds the human mind. The Master said: "Not even intending to strike the grass... [He continued with] Dahui, who said:

As soon as the snake is startled—(looking at the assembly, he says)—It is not that it is not so; it is that it is so. There is no need to weary the human mind with "nothingness.

The donor requests the Master to ascend the seat. [The Master] cites the occasion when Panshan was escorting a funeral procession. He heard a songster say: "The red wheel is certain to sink toward the west;
I wonder in which direction the soul has departed? Upon hearing the mournful wailing of the filial son, he attained enlightenment at that very moment.
The Master’s verse says: “The dew on the leeks is chilling and truly pitiable; The white poplars and crimson banners depart with fluttering grace.
Within the sound of mournful wailing there is no news; Striking the south, it moves the north.”
Ascending the hall after recovering from illness: Coming and going with illness brings only desolation; when the root of the disease is removed, the ailments multiply.
Over time, things undergo many changes; as one grows old, they become demons. Observe this—what will happen next?

Abbot’s Quarters.
Lift with one hand; grasp with the other. A hair’s breadth of difference, and heaven and earth lie between.
To grasp at anything other than this single reality is not true; this alone is the one fact. (Handing the commentary to the monk, he said: It is hidden within you. I—
To say it is not secret is incorrect;
this Dharma seat is the lion throne of the village. Yet, one cannot avoid being outmaneuvered by the shifting of circumstances, playing with the real as if it were false. Right now, who is there?
This is the bystander.

Grasping the mainstay, movement is like drifting clouds; the drifting clouds have no mind. Coming to rest is like the valley spirit; the valley spirit does not die. Thus movement and stillness coexist.
Stillness merges with movement; the two aspects of movement and stillness are clearly seen as non-arising.

To speak in such a manner is not only like sitting beneath the cliffs of Putuo Mountain waiting for a rabbit by its old stump; it also fails to avoid mistaking Master Duan’s lyrics for the "Pozhenzi" (Array of Troops) song.
Since they are neither lyrics nor a musical tune, when the smoke has vanished and the sun has risen and no one is to be seen, a single cry of "Kuai-nai" echoes from the mountain.
Shuilü: Again, he raised the case where Layman Pang asked Master Mazu, "Who is it that does not take the myriad dharmas as his companion?
The Master said, "I will tell you right now: he is one who can swallow up the waters of the West River in a single gulp. The Master [Zhaozhou] composed a verse on this:

The tracks of birds vanish across a thousand peaks; the footprints of men are extinguished for ten thousand *li*. An old man with a straw raincoat and hat on a small boat, fishing alone amidst the snow of the cold river.
Ascending the hall, he said: "In other quarters they speak of Chan; at Dizang’s place, they plant fields. But here, under my gate, it is otherwise:
when hungry, one eats; when weary, one sleeps. Those who are not true connoisseurs labor in vain discussing the rigors of winter."
Ascending the hall on the first day of the fourth month in the fourteenth year: flowing water is without sentiment; falling flowers leave no trace.
A single phrase, clearly realized, transcends ten billion worlds. Do not wait for the future to question Maitreya.
The Bathing of the Buddha: Ascending the Dharma Hall. Drawing well-water of the *jinhua* (well-flower) variety and boiling rose-essence, the pure *dharmakāya* is stained and defiled.
(After a long silence, he says: In this unruly world, this occurs once every year.
Ascending the hall, [the Master said]: "Three parts of time have already passed; the subsequent text is long. That single point in the numinous mind is never wiped away.
Since there is no wound there, one needlessly pursues life day by day, wandering aimlessly all day long. Even if you call out, they do not turn their heads—what can be done?
That matter is beyond hindrance. But tell me, what is that matter? (After a long silence, he said: "It cannot be lifted on a spoon."
Ascending the hall on the first day of the New Year: The old year has already passed; the first day of the new year is auspicious. At this very time today, we arrive at the first chapter.
Beidjian shall now meet with you all at the second head. What follows is a long discourse, to be entrusted to a future day.
Ascending the hall: On the fifteenth day of the third month, fallen blossoms and drifting floss fill the air; the consciousness of karma is vast and boundless, with no foundation upon which to rely.
To grasp it firmly and maintain mastery—only a quick-witted monk would not proceed in such a manner.

Ascending the hall, [the Master] raised this passage: The Buddha told the Bodhisattva Universal Eye, "Is there anyone who can explain, within the context of written words, the locus where the various illusory manifestations of illusion reside?
He replied, "No. The Buddha said, "Universal Eye, these are illusory manifestations within illusion."

It is already impossible to describe; how much more so the secret body-realm, secret speech-realm, and secret mind-realm of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva—to enter therein, to be able to enter, and to be able to see. The Master’s verse says: "Brilliantly it dwells in the heart and mind;
Luminously it resides amidst the objects of form. Do not mistake the silver world For a city of false silver."
Ascending the hall on the Lantern Festival: "I see that the lamp-light Buddha’s original radiance and auspicious signs are like this. As for the mountains, rivers, and great earth;
light and darkness, form and emptiness; the myriad phenomena of the universe; and even the lanterns and the pillars—all of them manifest this original radiance and auspicious signs.
Yet why is it that beneath the feet of you all there is such pervasive darkness?"

When Master Furong arrived, he ascended the hall and said: "Limping and dragging along, a hundred uglinesses and a thousand clumsinesses—vying for victory over all quarters and surpassing the inferiority of all quarters.
Even so, before those with clear eyes, one is utterly rendered tongue-tied and unable to strike a blow; there is no reason that can be extended.
Furthermore, where could anything be more unambiguous than this?"

Ascending the hall, the Master raised the following case: At the Huayan Assembly, the great Bodhisattvas could not see Samantabhadra. The Buddha instructed them to seek him through focused visualization, and they saw him immediately.
The Master composed a verse: “How many tongues does Gautama have? How many eyes do those in the assembly possess?
In every head and every object, In every land and every speck of dust— To deceive oneself is still tolerable; But the greatest suffering is deceiving others.”

Buddha Hall.

Ascending the hall, the Master raised the following case: Baofu asked Ehu, "Setting aside for a moment meeting at Wangzhou Pavilion or at Wushan Ridge, how about meeting before the Sangha Hall?
Ehu strode back to his quarters, and Baofu immediately entered the Sangha Hall. The Master commented:
"These two venerable elders had plenty to observe before the Sangha Hall; had they been able to draw the bowstring and release the arrow..."
When the trigger is pulled and the arrow hits the mark simultaneously, even if one has reached Wàngzhōu Pavilion, there is still Wūshí Lǐng ahead.

yet by the time they arrive, it is the Great Sage who is looking at the people of Sīzhōu. The head monks are on the west side, while the administrative officers are on the east.
Introduction: The incense burner and the lantern abide according to the Dharma; are they ultimately the same as when one has not yet stepped through the gate, or are they two different things?
(After a long silence, he says: It is difficult to deceive the eyes of the assembly.

Ascending the hall, [the Master said]: "The family of patch-robed monks is not merely elegant; they resent praise and cherish abuse. As for the samādhi of non-contention, those who truly know it are few.
Setting aside this samādhi for a moment, what is non-contention? When a guest arrives, one must receive them; when a thief arrives, one must strike them."
Ascending the hall, [the Master said]: "In various quarters they discuss Chan; Dizang plows his fields—these are but one-sided views.
Zhaozhou drinking tea and Heyuan beating the drum are unfit for conversation. Here, in my place, there is no 'accepting responsibility. Family disgrace has been needlessly broadcast abroad."
Ascending the hall for the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* assembly: The treasury of the *Lotus Sūtra* is profound, firm, remote, and far-reaching;

even the keen hearing of Shiqi Kuang could not hear it, nor the clear vision of Li Lou could see it. The South Mountain is radiant, its white stones glowing bright; the single assembly on Vulture Peak remains solemnly without dispersing.
Ascending the hall, [the Master] cited the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*: "A Bodhisattva takes the bodhicitta as their home; taking practice according to reality as their family dharma.

The Master said, "Let us set aside for a moment the matter of 'home. What is the family dharma? He then offered this verse: Roaming recklessly atop the tower, without restraint, Ling-ding Li-di, a pitiable creature.
The Akṣa-vinīta village is the entry into this very midst; The Son of the Buddha dwells not in a fixed place.
At another location, he ascended the hall and cited the *Dharmadhātu-vipaśyanā*: "The Dharmakāya flows through the five paths of rebirth and is called 'sentient beings.

Thus, when sentient beings manifest, the Dharmakāya does not manifest. The Master then offered this verse: "The Buddha’s true Dharmakāya— To the very end, it is but a fabrication. It sells itself for its own price."
Village wine. Holding a porcelain flask himself, he put on his robe and came forward as the host.
Ascending the hall, he raised an example: "Suppose there were a great scripture scroll, equal in measure to the three thousandfold world system, contained within a single speck of dust;
so it is with every speck of dust. There is a person of keen wisdom whose pure eyes can see it all. Breaking open the speck of dust, they bring forth the scripture scroll, providing vast abundance."
"To benefit sentient beings. The Master picked up the case and said: "If you intend to break a single atom, you are clearly ignorant of this sutra.
How can one break a scroll of scripture to produce this single atom?"

Ascending the hall upon his attainment of the Way, he said: "When malevolent stars descend upon the palace of one's destiny, the mountains are heavy with snow and cold, and the eyes grow dull with folly.
I am like a guest upon a fishing boat; I shall further inform you of this with a *kalāpa*."
Ascending the hall: It rains day after day; it rains night after night. The sun is locked away and the moon’s door is closed. The rice is ruined; the wheat is ruined.
But as for whether this very thing is ruined or not—ask the Mad Bag of Mingzhou.
Ascending the hall, [the Master] cited Master Xiu, who said: "When the sun rises, the light of the mind shines; when the sky is overcast, the ground-nature is dark.

He further said: "The myriad dharmas are the light of the mind; all conditions are but the clarity of nature. Often, various skillful means refer to Master Xiu as one who speaks of "mind" and "nature.
But how about Beijian? (Looking at the assembly, he said: "Who dares to give him a name?"
[Master] Zi ascended the hall and said: "Walking is Chan; sitting is Chan. When hungry, eat rice; when weary, sleep.
Three times he went to Touzi, nine times he ascended to Dongshan—needlessly digging in the earth to seek the blue sky."

[the Master] ascended the hall for the formal sermon. He cited the occasion when Bo-shan ascended the hall and, holding his staff horizontally across his chest, said: "It is not that in recent years..."
Exhorting him to drink: "Since we parted, it has been difficult to see you. Although Boshan is vast in land and sparse in people, those who meet there are few;
it is not so at the gate of Zhangjiao. There, the Way is cut off and the people are wild; one has not yet reached even half [of the realization]."

Chan Master Qian presided over the hall for the reception of guests. Facing Mount Lu at his gate, with the riverbanks overflowing the marshes, he firmly guards the vital ford where even crows cannot fly across.
He takes food and gives it to others to eat; tell me, is this a kind heart or not?
The waves of the Yangtze River are not yet deep.
When the news of the passing of Master Zongyuan and his secular elder brother arrived, he ascended the hall. A messenger came from Huangchi reporting, "Yesterday, my elder brother died.
Then another came from Pingjiang reporting, "This morning, my younger brother passed away. Ancient worthies used such things as paired sayings, but Zhangjiao took them as the true Dharma.
Why did Zhangjiao of great and small stature take them as the true Dharma? (Pointing to the meditation seat, he said: "If it were for the sake of teaching..."
Frequently shedding tears—the vast ocean must surely dry up.
Lifting the lament: "When dead, one is buried; when dead, one is buried. Originally there is no fixed rank; monks follow worldly arrangements.
Red Hongya, White Hongya—these are my kinsmen, all equally clever. Alas, alas!
On the occasion of the Winter Solstice, he ascended the hall. He raised the following case: Guishan asked Yangshan, "The bitter cold of mid-winter is an annual occurrence;
as the movement of the sun's shadow shifts, what is the matter? Yangshan stepped forward, joined his palms, and stood there.
Guishan said, "I knew you could not answer this question. Xiangyan said, "I am uniquely able to answer this question. Guishan asked, "How would you do it?"

Xiangyan joined his palms and stepped back to stand. The Master remarked, "In exerting the mechanism of splitting the bamboo and employing the 'precipice phrase,' these two disciples were not lacking;
yet, as for their answers, it was like trying to fit a square block into a round hole."
Ascending the hall, [the Master] raised the following case: Xuan Sha asked Elder Xiaotang, "Yesterday there was a great commotion;
where did it go? Xiaotang lifted the corner of his *kāṣāya*. Xuan Sha said, "I suspect there is no connection. The Master commented:
"The two elders knew only 'today' and 'tomorrow,' yet they were unaware of 'early autumn' and 'late autumn. Bei Jian, however, is not like this: today..."
Silent and still. Yesterday was a clamor and din. When the wind ceases, the flowers still fall; when the birds cry out, the mountains become even more secluded. Entering the hall, [the Master said]:
"Letting go at the precipice—only one who is willing can take it up. To revive after being cut off is something that cannot deceive you.
Therefore it is said: 'I stand here on the ground waiting for you to penetrate through. (He hurls down the staff and says: What kind of bowl are you looking for?"
