Buddha Hall.
No ritual is performed; ritual would surely be destroyed. A thousand people come, ten thousand bow. The Yellow-Faced Gautama eats this one thing and understands it.
In the abbot’s quarters, moving freely in all directions—thousandfold layers, hundredfold circuits—the true command is fully upheld. This scheme is not accepted. (A shout.)
This Dharma seat is far too small compared to those in other quarters. Today, we cannot help but manifest the great within the small. Look, look!
It is fundamentally and naturally so; it is not the work of the Arhats of Yunju.
The golden lion’s frame is of iron spine and iron waist, stubborn and unyielding; though he follows the ranks and the crowd, it is difficult for him to bend his joints.

If you wish to strike him as he passes beneath the gate of this monk, you must avoid some heat and endure some cold. If you wish to see one who avoids the heat and endures the cold, look for that fellow with the long neck.
When the *mò* and *lán* trees grow into a dense grove, one departs to become a guest at the Golden Phoenix Gate; yet how many do not fail at their beginning?

When taro is roasted over a fire of dung, who would recognize the purple seal of the Emperor’s decree? If one’s defenses are not tight, do not bring disputes to judge me; the worldly life of fabrication has nothing to do with this.
Sitting fully within the midst of right and wrong, one is nonetheless known by the world for where one dwells. This old monk is clear—!
The sun shifts its dwelling once more; the numinous tortoise drags its tail away. The ancients have already shattered [the world] all at once.
As for the model of Beijian—who is a true connoisseur? One song, two songs—no one understands them. After the rain has passed, the autumn waters in the night pond are deep.
The news of the passing of Master Gao Yuan arrived. He ascended the hall and said: "On the eleventh day of the second month, someone came from North Mountain to report that Gao Yuan is dead.
For a monk such as this, one only suffers from having too much, not too little. Tsk! Seek another like him—like the moon among the stars, like gold in the sand;
he is nowhere to be found, even if you sift through the earth and stir up the dust."
Ascending the hall: To seize the tiger’s head and gather up its tail—such a person has yet to be seen. To clarify the fundamental principle beneath the first phrase—I have heard its words before.
He kicks it up and goes; white clouds ten thousand miles away.
The monks of the two parishes returned to their home villages. Entering the hall, [the Master said:
"Those who knew they were mistaken even before setting foot southward—some fifteen pairs of them—often turned away from the truth right before their faces, refusing to accept it.

Had they not followed the error with more error, they would have avoided adding frost to snow. Here in my place, I shall prune and edit the path. (He threw down the staff and said: "Listen to the smoke and oars!"

Ascending at Qutang Gorge for the Lantern Festival, the Master addressed the assembly: "The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa* contains the Dharma-gate of the 'Inexhaustible Lamp. In later generations, those of clever ingenuity have taken this and elaborated upon it:

one lamp and ten mirrors, ten mirrors and one lamp, their lights interlacing and reflecting one another, so that even when interrogated, no trace remains. Yet the mirror is simply the mirror, and the lamp is simply the lamp."
The lamp of self: the master blows it out and walks in the dark.
When the Buddha enters Nirvana, he ascends the hall; the failure lies at the Twin Trees. There is no trace whatsoever to be found; when the ocean dries up, its bottom is finally seen.
When a person dies, they do not know where their mind has gone.
When Master Mingqing arrived, he ascended the hall and said: "When a thief comes, one must strike; when a guest comes, one must receive them. Elder Mingqing has come."
Striking is it; receiving is it. If he strikes and comes forward, no stolen goods are seen; if he receives and comes forward, the origins have not yet been questioned.
Enough, enough! Were it not for an old grudge, we would not have met head-to-head.
Ascending the hall on the first day of the New Year: The new year begins its reign; all things are renewed. On this very day, I humbly reflect:
the True Person of No Rank—when full, do not rejoice; when hungry, do not resent. For one day, from head to foot, five *he* of plain rice.

Ascending the hall, he cited the *Nirvāṇa-parivarta* of the *Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment*: "Abiding at all times, do not give rise to deluded thoughts; yet do not attempt to extinguish those deluded minds.
Abiding within the realm of deluded thoughts, do not apply further discernment; in this absence of discernment, do not seek to distinguish the real.

The Master composed a verse: A small boat moored between the two banks amidst the forest trees; In the whistling wind, my two temples are swept by white hair. I attend to nothing of the myriad affairs, for I am drunk.
Awakening once more, he dwells forever amidst the misty waves, playing with the bright moon.

He ascends the hall to address the new and old orders of the community. Measuring talent to fill offices, cultivating virtue to enjoy leisure—whether in motion or stillness, he wondrously turns the pivot of the mechanism.
Its brilliance illuminates heaven and mirrors the earth; who is permitted to behold it?
On the eighth day of the fourth month, he ascended the hall: The formless body of empty space falls to the ground, stirring up dust and grime.
If it does not enter the midst of the red dust, when—like a donkey’s year—will it ever be washed clean?
The Discourse Record of Chan Master Chongming of Biyun Temple in Changzhou,
Compiled by Daguang for the Purpose of Study.
Three Sections.
Lohan Mountain stands directly opposite the entrance; at dawn, sacred lamps appear. The barriers between high and low have all been shattered; no distinction is made even for monks of the Hīnayāna.
In the Buddha Hall, one sees earthen niches; one bows to these earthen niches and likewise pays homage to the clay statues. Two thousand years since the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, bhikṣus are few.
Shame and remorse!
A single shot from the abbot’s quarters hits the mark; a hundred shots pierce the bullseye. At the crossroads of Biyun, yet another of the "Three Harms" has been added.
[The Master] holds up the citation (and says to the assembly): "This is the venerable elder Jinshen. He is the Censor Wang Wanniun of Changzhou, whom ten thousand oxen could not turn back.
A single drop of ink from his brush is scattered across the azure clouds; in both places, he has become a dragon. [He] departs.
"There is a single point of spiritual affinity that penetrates all.
Entering the hall, he said: "The sun may grow cold and the moon may grow hot; no demons can destroy the True Teaching. But tell me, what is the True Teaching?
Three people testify that this is certainly not a turtle—it is a tortoise."
Ascending the hall, he said: "The ten directions gather together; each dreams upon the same bed. Every one studies non-action; there is no wound there.
This is the field for selecting Buddhas, a land of pestilence and poison. With an empty mind, one returns with the highest degree.
Returning is not non-existent, but can the single phrase of 'arriving home' be heard? (He struck the meditation staff and said: "To turn one's head back, one still remains halfway."
Ascending the hall, [the Master] cited Emperor Xiaozong’s question to Chan Master Fozhao: "What did Śākyamuni accomplish during his six years in the mountains?
Fozhao replied, "I thought Your Majesty had forgotten. The Master offered this verse: "Borrowing my mother-in-law's robe to bow for her birthday;
The ladle from the original edition cannot be lifted by Zen. Raising up the Jade Dragon, it thunders like a crash of lightning."
"The morning star still lingers in the ninefold heavens.
[The Master] ascends the hall. He cites the case where Huangbo sat in Nanquan’s place; Nanquan asked, "In what year did you, Elder, begin your practice?"
Huangbo said, "Before King Bhīṣmagarjitasvaranāda. Nanquan said, "That is still the descendant of Old Master Wang. Huangbo then returned to the second seat.
The Master [Zhaozhou] commented: "Huangbo descended from the seat; Nanquan ascended the seat. Paper is in high demand in Changzhou; one document covers it all."
Ascending the hall, he brought up the story of Zhaozhou visiting Touzi. He commented: "Glistening and smooth. Like sounds responding to one another and essences seeking their kin.
His golden armor has been honed through a hundred battles; his iron whip is full of strength, yet he harbors a grudge for having no enemy."
Ascending the hall on the first day of the New Year: "The pillar keeps watch through the night; The lantern pays its respects at dawn.
The black staff joins the procession without a record to show; It leaps out from the left side of the meditation seat. Universally extending greetings and blessings, following the search:
May you enjoy a thousand autumns. Born with wealth and honor—take care not to seek it elsewhere. (He strikes the sounding block and says: "Good news!"
Ascending the hall: What others discard, I take up; what others take up, I give away. Playing with the mass of karmic consciousness, there is no fundamental basis to rely upon.
To destroy the Buddha and slander the Dharma is to fall outside the ranks of the assembly. Though it is clearly before one's eyes, it is difficult to distinguish the black from the white.
Ascending the hall: The Buddha-dharma of the three periods of time—three periods do not understand it. The Buddha-dharma of the six patriarchs—the six patriarchs do not understand it.
The Buddha-dharma of the old monks throughout the world—the old monks throughout the world do not understand it. How shameful! As for the Buddha-dharma of the various mountains at present—
There is nothing he does not penetrate; there is nothing he does not know. How truly marvelous! "The traveler on the road has a mouth like a stone monument.
[He] ascended the hall and cited Master An’s reading of the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* by breaking the phrasing. The Master offered this verse: "Before reaching the stage where one forgets the trap..."
Carrying his basket and other gear, he leaps like a shrimp; taking a wrong path through the woods, he arrives at the home of Ge Hong.
Ascending the hall, he said: "In the Western Heaven, they use a wax man as a test. How about here in this land? It depends on the abundance or scarcity of one's household.
Ultimately, what serves as the test? The sword that kills, the sword that gives life."
Ascending the hall, he said: "The dragon does not recognize the sword, yet it dies beneath the blade; the tiger does not recognize the pit, yet it dies within the trap.
Fish take water as their life—why then do they die within the water? Because of walking, one need not hinder the swinging of one's arms."
Ascending the hall, [the Master said: "Luzu would simply turn his back to the wall upon seeing a monk. 'Throughout my life, I have laid my liver and gall bare before others.
I, the decrepit Beijian, have neither back nor face; I shall never act as an intermediary for you. Let the blue seas change as they may."
Upon receiving the news of the passing of the Venerable Master Fusheng Tan, he ascended the hall. Someone asked, "The Chan Master Dadao of Fusheng has passed away;
where has he gone? He replied to him: "A muddy pig and a scabby dog have no desire to be born in heaven. A true practitioner extinguishes the barbarian seed;
as for becoming a Buddha, wait until donkey year."
Ascending the hall: On the first day of the last month of winter—look, look! It is already the thirtieth day of the twelfth lunar month, what is called the "head of the year.
It is also called the "ultimate point. Is there anyone who can turn their body here?
If there is, they will eat their rice in Silla and take their meal at Shaolin. If not yet so, then south of the Heavenly Terrace and north of the Five Terraces.
Ascending the hall: "Drops dripping from the eaves—clear and distinct. You, O monk with clear eyes, (striking the staff) must by all means avoid entering through this door."

The Empress Dowager has ascended to heaven; I ascend the hall. In the deep chambers of Changle Palace, the water-clock drips slowly. At the third watch of the night, I ponder deeply for my family’s sake.
The bells toll and the clock runs out as the Dragon Tower dawns; there will be no more time when the "Cock-man" asks after the Emperor's rest.
Ascending the hall on the first day of the third month: Spring is already past its midpoint. A monkey is tied to a dew-pillar; the dew-pillar calls out with every sound.
"The South Mountain is bright, the white stones are worn away. (He strikes the meditation staff and says: "As for this one point, when has it ever been worn away?"

Ascending the hall, he raised the *Niyatārtha-parivarta* chapter of the *Awakening of Faith in the Mahāyāna*, saying: "If this contemplation cannot be attained, one should again practice that contemplation, never letting the mind abandon its focus, gradually seeking realization.
(He struck the meditation staff. "Upon hearing this, the meditation staff could not help but laugh aloud, and immediately spoke this incantation:"
"The gate of the three contemplations has opened; I shall universally request that you be buried alive. I stand here on this very ground waiting for you to pass through—how could you deceive me?
(He threw down his staff and descended from the seat.)
Ascending the hall, the Master raised the following case: When Mañjuśrī held up a crystal cup and asked Wuzhuo, "Is there such a thing as this in the South?
Wuzhuo replied, "No. Mañjuśrī said, "Then with what do you drink your tea? Wuzhuo was speechless. Master Baoning Yong, acting on behalf of Wuzhuo, pointed his finger at his own mouth.
The Master commented: "If it were Beijian, he would have simply taken the tea and drunk it."
Ascending the hall: Fishing alone upon the autumnal seas and mountains, The line and rod weigh fifty catties. I caution you, oysters and clams: Do not approach the hook that catches the giant turtle.
Shifting the Buddha to the hall: Shifted to the east, then shifted back to the west; Does the Immovable Honored One ever move? [He] does not strike.
Sitting together with others in a squatting posture, who knows that the forty-nine years were not [merely] so?
Chengdao ascends the hall: The cold freezes to the bone and the eyes cannot open; from where does this single spark of Yanghe come?
Six years of bitter toil have all been brought to rest; failing to realize the morning star was the source of calamity.

When acting as the *karmadāna* (venerable attendant) and serving in the hall, one responds three times and calls out three times; entering the weeds without complaint, being fined, and expelled from the monastery—these are precisely for the purpose of putting the teaching into practice.
As for the stubborn and willful attendant, Menglang Kebin said: "The sound of the Qiang flute reaches the evening at the farewell pavilion;
you head toward Xiangxiang, while I go toward Qin."
Ascending the hall on the Double Fifth: Today, in all quarters, some are writing talismans and others are gathering medicinal herbs;
the azure clouds are parched with exhaustion and the hungry clamor for food. This one single point—set it all aside with total abandon! (After a long pause, he says: With eyes open, it is right;
with eyes closed, it is right.
Ascending the hall, he said: "One person is always on the road, yet never leaves home; another person leaves home, yet is not on the road.
How can one express the 'hand-receiving' phrase? From south to north, from west to east."
Record of the Sermons at Huiri Chan Monastery in Chushu County, Pingjiang Prefecture.
Compiled by the student Da-guan. Recorded by the Librarian Zangzhu.
Ascending the Dharma Hall: The deep resentment for the cup of ginger and apricot has not yet been dispelled; the bamboo oar is treated as something trivial.
Shake it! Once you have withdrawn the waves, who is there to learn to play in the tide at the hollow of the shore? Therefore it is said:
"If you are not one who plays in the tide, do not enter the great surging waves. You must possess his spiritual power; only when your turning wheels roll freely can you succeed.
But tell me, do they turn left or right? (A shout.)
Opening the furnace, he ascends the hall. He cites Xuefeng’s address to the assembly: "The world is one chi wide; the ancient mirror is one chi wide.
The world is ten feet wide; the ancient mirror is ten feet wide. Xuansha pointed at the brazier and said, "I wonder how wide this one is?
Xuefeng replied, "As wide as the ancient mirror. The Master comments: "Xuefeng [was among] the fifteen hundred..."
A person’s true spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) takes their credibility from the *zhang* (measuring staff). Throughout the world and for all future generations, none dare not to believe them.
Yet if one says they are as broad as an ancient mirror, none dare not to doubt them. (Zhuo strikes the staff and says: "If you doubt, go elsewhere; otherwise, consult the Head Seat.
Upon entering the hall, he said: "The former Buddha Zhao said: 'At the stroke of the staff, one encounters a living Chan monk; this is the True Dharma Eye.'"
Zangzeng increased the price; Beijian was not so. With a single blow from his staff, he struck the living monk, causing the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye to crumble like tiles and melt like ice.
Tell me, is this the same as the former Buddha Zhao, or is it different?
He ascended the hall on account of a specific matter: "A single palm does not sound recklessly; a single thread does not form a line.

These are matters concerning the general communal labor (*pǔqǐng*) practiced in various quarters. However, within the gate of Huiri, it is precisely required that a single thread form a line and a single palm sound itself.
Only when the night is deep will one see the person holding the needle.
Ascending the hall, [the Master] raised the case of Elder Mi and Dongshan while they were at a pancake shop.
Elder Mi drew a circle on the ground and said to Dongshan, "Take this away. Dongshan replied, "Bring it here. Later, Zen Master Baoning Yong said:
Not only these two men cannot lift it up; even all the people of the entire earth cannot lift it up. Beigan dares to say:
Baoning’s resources were exhausted and his strength spent.
Ascending the hall, [the Master] raised an ancient saying: "This mind is still not yet resolved; even a drop of water is difficult to digest.

Beijian, however, did not say it this way: "What need is there for this mind to be resolved? Even a drop of water is not difficult to digest. Now tell me, is he close to the ancients or distant from them?
(The Master of the Hall said: "The purpose of raising chickens is for the early hours of the fifth watch;

today we thank the new and old orders as they ascend the hall. Do not keep your hands in your sleeves like a general who has lowered his flag; together let us support this broken-legged cauldron. When the high game is played, lower your move;
where there is a dead path, teach it to become alive."

Xie Ding ascends the hall for the first seat. The matters of the ancestors that transcend the school and surpass the conventional—if one does not possess the skillful hands and feet of a pig-eater or dog-biter, how can one perceive them with the true eye?
It is like a lute, a zither, or a harp; though they possess exquisite sounds, if there are no skilled fingers, [the music cannot be produced].

In the end, they were unable to produce a sound. Once the subtle fingers were struck, the subtle tones became dense and perfect; ten thousand apertures fell silent, and even walls and partitions seemed to have ears.
What need was there for a pure breeze to stir the heavens and earth?
The Bathing of the Buddha: Ascending the Dharma Hall. With a single "wa," he lets out a roar; suddenly there emerges such a great icchantika.
From this land and from the Western Heaven, calamity and harm arise. Magnificent and imposing, he washes the earth, yet it does not turn to mud.
Ascending the hall, [the Master said: "In the past, there was a scholar who composed a 'Treatise on the Non-existence of Ghosts. A ghost appeared and said, 'You say there are no ghosts;
what about me? The scholar then set down his pen. If Beijian had seen him speak in such a manner, he would have simply said to him:
'I took you for a human being, but it turns out you are also a ghost.'"
Ascending the hall, [the Master] cited Xiangyan’s saying: “Last year’s poverty was not yet true poverty; it was like eating sugarcane upside down.
This year’s poverty is truly poverty; one gradually enters the refined state. Last year’s poverty still left room enough to stick a锥 (chui—a small awl);
one could still manage without relying on family wealth. This year’s poverty leaves no room even for a 锥; you poor ghosts, you are truly happy to the point of exhaustion. Yangshan called out.
He performed the Tathāgata-dhyāna. "Thief! Thief! This year, the Sun of Wisdom has become even more precarious. The traveler is now beyond the green mountains.
Upon receiving the news of the passing of West Hall Master Gaosue Xi of Jingshan, he ascended the hall and said: "The single bubble of Gaosue Xi has vanished, rolling into the dragon pool."

Inside, the Dragon Pool is stirred until turbid; in the sixth month, the ice remains frozen to the bottom. Before the He-shi Rock, in the fields of calamus, the fool still scoops out water from the night pond.
Master Zhao ascends the hall upon returning to his hometown: Coming, he regrets leaving the capital too late; returning, he regrets entering the gorges too late.

He suspects that his present realization is genuine, yet wonders if his past state was not already enlightened. Seeking south was delusion; visiting north was likewise false. At twilight, the azure clouds merge together.
Amidst the chaotic mountains, the cuckoo cries.
Entering the hall, [the Master said]: "In such heat as this, there is nowhere to be found that is not hot. Ten thousand miles east and west, eighty thousand miles north and south."
Wandering everywhere and coming and going is not as good as staying here. But tell me, what kind of realm is this? When Beijian arrived here, he himself did not know it.
(He strikes the meditation staff and says: "The one in the midst of the game is lost.
For the sake of the deceased monk, he ascends the hall and cites a monk who asked Dalong: "When the physical body decays, what is the indestructible dharma?"
Shenlong said: "The mountain flowers bloom like brocade; the stream water is as clear as indigo. This is the decay of the form-body (*rūpakāya*).
What is the steadfast Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) of Chan Shouzuo? The sun is at its zenith; the fragrant breeze comes from the south."
Record of the Sayings of Husheng Wansui Chan Monastery on Mount Daochang, Anji Prefecture, Compiled by Daguān, a Student of the Dharma.
Incense Offering for the Memorial of Fozhao: "Rough, rough!
When the crude is exhausted, the clever arises; it is a scene of total failure. At times, one realizes the transformation of a turtle into a snake."

The tortoise: Suddenly he has proven the tortoise to be a turtle. All the sons know how to spend their father’s money; this unworthy son of the "tortoise-nest" claps his hands and laughs until the heavens tremble.
He laughs at him for playing with it all the way before the Emperor.

Ascending the hall, [the Master] said: "The world is fundamentally without affairs; it is only the common person who disturbs it. It is like a Wheel-Turning King (Cakravartin) who rules over the great chiliocosm.
When various petty kings refuse to submit, and the king’s generals achieve merit in battle, he bestows rewards according to their service:

elephants, horses, chariots, gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and even the bright pearl from his topknot—he gives these to them as well. I ask you, the assembly: what alone does the King keep for himself?"
Above this is a single pearl; for what reason, then, do you also give it to him? (Master Zhuo says: To establish the foundation of Great Peace amidst the chaos of war.
Entering the hall through the snow: if there is even one dharma, Vairocana falls into the rank of ordinary beings; if there are not ten thousand dharmas, Samantabhadra...
He lost his realm; his eyes were filled with a world of silver, and everywhere was Samantabhadra.
But tell me, did Puyan see it or not?
He ascended the hall and said: "Last year’s plum blossoms, this year’s willows—the heavens and earth have performed their full work, and every thing remains as it was. O patch-robed monks!
His life remains as it was before. With three or five pecks of green ash upon his head, between the winter snows and the spring winds, do not let the opportunity slip away at the edge of the mattock.
When news arrived of the passing of the venerable master from the Guishan Hermitage of Zhaojue, he ascended the hall and said: "A single oar flies across the Ghost Gate Barrier."
Beyond the Pass lies the sky; Jiuhua is the most excellent place under heaven. Seizing the moment to behold it amidst the snow, the azure clouds merge at dusk;
cloud and monk are both at ease. Meeting by chance here in this very spot—tell me, is this life or death? It is difficult for the eyes of the multitude to deceive.
Ascending the hall, [the Master] raised an example: "When Dahui was serving as a secretary in the capital, Yuanwu constantly kept him by his side.
One day, while Yuanwu was holding chopsticks before a guest, Dahui involuntarily stared with wide-open eyes. Yuanwu said, 'This fellow has attained a kind of "yellow-amber wood Zen.
The Master commented: "How Yuanwu, great as he was, pulled up the seedlings to help them grow!"

Ascending the hall on the anniversary of the Emperor’s birthday: The eight directions submit to his benevolence; the One Man has cause for celebration. The woodcutter’s song and the fisherman’s chant—every beat is the Imperial Decree.
But what tune is it, after all? (Striking the meditation seat with his hand, he says: “Ten Thousand Years of Joy.”
Ascending the hall: This morning is the fifth day of the third month. The weather is half-sunny and half-rainy. In the gardens and groves, Qingming has passed;
countless fallen flowers and drifting floss fill the air. Śākyamuni is stingy; Maitreya is wealthy. Most pitiable is the cuckoo, who knows not the season;
it cries until its throat bleeds, yet its song is of no use.
Ascending the hall, he said: "Three months of spring have passed until this very morning at the first watch of the fifth hour;
there has not been even a hair’s breadth left to manage. But tell me, by what principle does one proceed in such a manner? (He struck the meditation staff and said: "The meditation staff says:
Two clay oxen fight their way into the sea, and until this very day there has been no news. How profoundly true! How profoundly true! I dare guarantee it."

It has not yet been fully penetrated. The *huāpúguā* (flower papaya) is truly extraordinary. It is said: "The waters of Chicken Island have no lid" (as the Master strikes the sounding block and descends from his seat).
When the elder master Huì of Bǎoíng arrived, he ascended the hall and cited the verse composed by Master Yǒng upon parting from his senior brother, Báiyún: [Verse omitted as per instructions]
Grasping the tangled vines, one cannot pull them apart. The old barbarian [Bodhidharma] debates length and shortness;
are the five Sumeru mountains high or not? Are the waters of the four great oceans full or not? Looking at it, these are also but tangled vines.

Today, having come from within the thicket of tangled vines, you have once again fallen into the thicket of Golden Peak. Why? The clouds and moon are the same; the streams and mountains are each different.
Ascending the hall, [the Master] raised an ancient case: A monk asked Dahui, "Who is it that does not take the myriad dharmas as a companion?
Dahui replied, "It is this person who is beyond the heavens above and the earth below, one for whom there is no recourse. The monk said, "How is it then that you are here under the seat at Jingshan?
Dahui answered, "If a household has no minor servants, it cannot be called a gentleman's home. "I, your unworthy grandson," [the Master] continued, "am not like that. If there should happen to be..."
Question: "Who is the one who does not take the myriad dharmas as his companion? I simply say to him: "The ladle cannot scoop it up.
How is it, then, that he is found beneath the Tiger Rock, north of the Stone Bridge, west of Nan-yuan, having searched through every cold branch yet refusing to perch?
Leaving the ranks to return to the hall: for half a month he was gone, his nostrils could not see his eyes; one day he returned, his eyes could not see his nostrils.
He lost his alertness and traded it for a collection of antiquities; yet though they are such, they remain nothing but a heap of rubbish.
The greedy do not give; the incorruptible do not take. (Master Zhuo says:

"Beating [the staff] back to the monastery for the commencement of the retreat, one ascends the hall for the ninety-day period of restraining the feet. What samādhi is this? They gather like a swarm of fireflies, falling eastward and collapsing westward."
Suddenly, as if two arrowheads were meeting point-to-point, [the truth] flashes forth from the eyes and strips away the skull.
Huyan said to him, "Not yet.
Ascending the hall, he cited Baguaoshan (Cloth Sack Monk), who was standing in the middle of a thoroughfare. A monk asked, "What are you doing? Baguaoshan replied:
"You are not that kind of person. (Do not let Fenghua [Huichao] take over. The monk says, "Come here. (The tattered sleeves. The monk in the cloth bag takes a tangerine and gives it to the monk.
(The thief’s loot is not accepted. As soon as the monk receives it, the one in the bag withdraws his hand and says, "You are not that kind of person."
Furthermore, as for one who has brought about transformation, the Master should not let him pass by.
When he says, "Wait for someone like me," the Master simply replies, "Thank you, Third Lady, for weighing the silver."
Record of the Sayings of Jingci Shan Baoen Guangxiao Chan Temple, Lin’an Prefecture.
Compiled by the student Da-guan.
Buddha Hall.
This knee has not bowed to others for a long time. For what reason today? The master’s manner is presented face-to-face;
one who possesses the virtue of benevolence does not yield.
The Abbot.
If one ascends to the top of nine fathoms, I must surely be there with them. If one reaches the bottom of the nine abysses, I shall likewise be there with them.
When I do not appear, why do you not see me? (A shout).
I offer this incense.
I reverently pray for the present Emperor that his sacred life-span may be boundless—ten thousand years, ten thousand years, ten thousand times ten thousand years! Next, I take up the incense.

[The Master] said: "This one portion of incense is offered for the Great Chancellor, Duke of the State, as well as the civil and military officials of the hundred ranks, to collectively augment their years of longevity. Again, picking up the incense, he said:
"This one portion of incense is offered for the Third [Honored One]."
The Imperial Decree: "The Five Abbot’s Quarters and the Meditation Halls have run amok, slaughtering the monks of the world.

Having previously resided at Mount Jing and now spending my final years on Mount Mao, I owe no gratitude to repay and no shame to expiate for my late master, the Venerable Dong’an; I shall offer this body and mind to serve every dust mote and land."

The method of ascending the seat does not arise in isolation; it arises only when confronted with the objective realm. Thus, one practices the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma, and the banner of the Dharma is established wherever one may be.
Therefore, Yongjia said: "To erect the banner of the Dharma and establish the fundamental principle—this is clearly the Buddha’s command at Caoxi. Yet, how could it be limited to Caoxi alone?
Within the three thousandfold world system, there is not even a space the size of a mustard seed that is not where a Bodhisattva has descended to be born.
He left the household life to cultivate the Way, turned the wheel of Dharma, and entered parinirvāṇa.
Now, at this very moment, he wishes to establish the school of Yangqi Baiyun, firmly planting the banner of victory so that even crows cannot fly across it.

He acts with one hand alongside those from the lakes and seas who destroy the Buddha and slander the Dharma—those icchantikas who are not counted among the ranks of the assembly. He has arisen from beneath my flower and papaya tree to clear away the heap of refuse.
"Head! The bright moon’s radiance shines upon heaven and earth. Suddenly, there is one who cannot restrain himself and comes forth, saying, 'It is indeed beautiful;

At the ends of the earth, news cannot pass; strength exhausted and spirit weary, there is nowhere to seek it. The Ten-Thousand-Year Pine stands upon Mount Zhurong.
The Master’s verse says:
"That which I formerly wished for, is now fulfilled. This jade is truly marvelous; yet I fear it may not be jade."
Raising the "Eight Returns" to Discern the Seeing. Wan’an’s Verse: Brightness, darkness, form, and emptiness cannot be returned; that which cannot be returned is beyond all climbing and grasping.
It carves out the void of space to form boundaries and shores: one layer of water separates one layer of mountain.
The Master’s Verse says:
Form, emptiness, brightness, and darkness each do not know one another. "When walking, I reach the end of the water;
sitting, I watch the clouds arise. [The text] cites Pūrṇa asking the Buddha: "If it is originally pure and fundamental, how is it that mountains, rivers, and the great earth suddenly arise?
Wanzan’s verse: "Originally pure and fundamental, pervading the Dharma-realm; mountains, rivers, and the great earth all manifest therein. The nature-awakening must..."
Recognizing the brightness within the shadow-brightness, the eyes and ears then follow along with sounds and forms. The Master’s verse says:
"Pervasive and pure, it ultimately admits nothing else; mountains, rivers, the great earth, and the myriad phenomena of the universe."
When the six are raised, the one is resolved and all is lost. Wan’an’s verse says: Roots and objects, bondage and liberation, originally share the same source.
Rest in one place and the six functions are abandoned. Holding a single strand of red thread, The nostrils of one’s birth-mother are pierced all at once.
The Master’s verse says:
Bondage and liberation are not distinct; existence and non-existence have no basis. Let us inquire into the fundamental source: who bound you in the first place?
[The Master] cites the thirty-two manifestations and fourteen fearlessnesses of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva from the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*.
Wanzan’s verse says: "The thirty-two manifestations are inconceivable; the fourteen fearlessnesses flow like water. (Male)
When entering meditative absorption within the body of a man, one emerges from that absorption within the body of a woman. The Master’s verse says:
"Turning the hand over makes clouds; covering the hand makes rain. The consciousness of karma is in a frantic rush, with no fundamental basis to rely upon."
Raising up the wondrous nature’s perfect clarity, it is free from all names and marks; fundamentally, there have never been worlds or sentient beings.
Wan’an’s Verse: “One coin as the capital, ten thousand coins as the profit; The rich are not enough, while the poor have a surplus.
A little medicine that changes the bones and seizes the womb— I must yield to Pan Lang riding his donkey backward. The Master’s Verse: The Master’s verse says:
The golden platter could not be moved; it rolled and turned, difficult to steady. After waiting for a long while, it became perfectly bright and as still as a dewdrop.

Then Ānanda and the great assembly again addressed the Buddha, saying: "If this wondrously bright, truly pure, and sublime mind is fundamentally pervasive and perfect—extending even to the great earth, grasses, trees, and all wriggling, sentient beings—if their original source is True Suchness (Tathatā), then..."
This is the true body of the Tathāgata’s attainment of Buddhahood. Since the Buddha-body is truly real, how can there still be hells, hungry ghosts, and animals?
Wan’an’s verse says: Before the Double Sword Peak lies the ruins of an ancient temple; the Celestial Honored One was originally but one Muni.
At such a time of difficulty, one can only share the incense and lamps. Do not listen to idle people as they speak of right and wrong.
The Master’s verse says: Three snakes and nine mice; within a single mu of land. Carrying dry wood with him, he performs his play upon meeting the stage.

The Buddha said: "Ānanda, these sentient beings do not recognize their original mind and undergo this cycle of rebirth for immeasurable kalpas, failing to attain true purity because they follow along with killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct.
By reversing these three, one gives rise to the absence of killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct.
That which has 'existence' is the realm of ghosts; that which has 'non-existence' is the celestial realm. Existence and non-existence oppose and displace one another."

The nature of saṃsāra arises. Wan’an’s Verse: "Refining the one deluded mind through the seven stations, Yet following the three karmas of killing, stealing, and lust— Body and mind are not merely tools for use;
The first arrow was light, but the subsequent arrows are deep. The Master’s Verse says:
I have stayed in guesthouses in Bingzhou for ten years now; my heart yearns to return, remembering Xianyang day and night.
Without cause, I have once again crossed the Sanggan River, and looking back toward Bingzhou, it is my true hometown.
As the Tathāgata himself, after describing the demons of dhyāna, told Ānanda: "Do not allow the demons of the mind to give rise to deep calamity.
Wanzan’s verse says: "Gautama’s thoroughgoing grandmotherly heart— Seeing light and the arising of form is difficult to bear in principle.
Entering the village and following local custom with nāga-samādhi— At this point, both Buddhas and demons sink away completely. The Master’s verse says:
To draw a bow, one must draw it taut; to use a spear, one must use a long one. To strike down a man, first strike his horse; to capture a rebel, first capture the king.

Ying’an raised this point to instruct the assembly, saying: "It is like a fine horse that moves at the mere sight of the whip’s shadow. Before he could finish, Fozhao stepped forward from the crowd and said: "One who moves at the sight of the whip’s shadow is not a fine horse. Ying’an then desisted. The Master offered this verse: To draw a bow, one must draw it taut; To use a spear, one must use a long one. To strike down a man, first strike his horse; To capture a rebel, first capture the king.
A fine horse moves at the sight of the whip’s shadow— But one who moves at the sight of the whip’s shadow is no fine horse. When Ying’an desisted, Fozhao was already far ahead.
The second head is like a swift flame passing through the wind; it cannot endure desolation, yet it can only endure sorrow.
After one cry of long neighing that shakes its mane, ten thousand horses fall silent as the battle is won.

Zhaozhou said, "I am in Qingzhou, making a robe of cotton cloth that weighs seven catties. The verse says:

Last year’s poverty was *Lei* (Thunder) above the heavens—*Zhuang* (Strength). This year’s poverty is *Meng* (The Stagnant) as water flows from beneath the mountain.
My family tradition is no different from that of Xiangyan; yet the iron cauldron for boiling tea is not the same.
Citing the story of Danxia visiting Layman Pang, the verse says:
The father is stubborn and lazy; the son repays the debt. This is the thoroughgoing mind of a grandmother: Red earth smeared upon the cow’s milk.
Citing the Case of Danxia Visiting National Teacher: The verse says:
A weasel that has gone weaning shows its fangs and claws; After Danxia departed, he spoke of Danxia.
If there is an eye upon the staff as bright as the sun, One must be an old master like Nanyang.
Raising up the story of Deshan’s beckoning across the river and Gaoting’s sudden dash across:
who across the river can recommend the "arrow-point" pivot? To dash straight across is already late. Regretfully, as the song ends, the person is gone;
the several peaks are carved from jade, and the waters flow vast and deep.
The *Complete Enlightenment Sutra* states: "At all times, do not give rise to deluded thoughts. Do not attempt to suppress or extinguish these deluded minds.
When abiding within the realm of deluded perceptions, do not apply analytical knowledge; and in the absence of such analytical knowledge, do not seek to discern what is real."
The three months of spring are no season for reading books; during the nine months of summer’s blazing heat, let Chan rest.
Only autumn and winter are somewhat better, yet it is not as good as passing the remaining years in sleep.

A monk asked Da-sui: "When the kalpa-fire blazes forth and the great trichiliocosm is utterly destroyed, as soon as you extend your question within the flames of that kalpa-fire, you immediately understand how to follow him away and then return. Having returned, you regret it at the path below the slope;
the chaotic mountains remain as ever, green and towering."
The King of Kaśmīra raised his sword and asked the Venerable Siṃha, "Have you realized the emptiness of the aggregates?
The Master replied, "I have realized the emptiness of the aggregates. "Have you transcended birth and death? The Master replied, "I have transcended birth and death. "Then give me your head."

The Venerable One said, "Even this body is not mine; how much less so my head? Thereupon, the King struck off the Venerable One's head, from which white milk gushed forth several *zhang* high, and the King's own arm fell off of its own accord.
Beneath the sword’s edge, there is tenfold intimacy; it is difficult to conceal, yet the body stands revealed alone. The river flows on, but the stone does not turn;
there is only the name “Embracing Emptiness. Master Jianben An said: "The teachers of all quarters bring forth only half of the green and yellow;
they all lack Wei Lang’s single night of frost. How can they compare to Yaoshan’s tonight? He places the whole platter before us, its fragrance naturally wafting forth."
In total, Wei Lang lacks one night’s frost; the various quarters pick out half-green and half-yellow. Azure clouds do not further nail onto the platter;
presenting this to the various quarters will only result in a round of laughter.
A monk asked an ancient worthy, "What is it like when the year is exhausted and the age comes to an end? The ancient worthy said, "The old Wang of East Village burns paper money at night.

"The old Wang of East Village burns paper money at night"—this is not Zen regarding the exhaustion of the year and the end of the age; it is the very message of the exhaustion of the year and the end of the age.
Separate. "The Old King of East Village Burns Paper Money at Night.
A verse sent to Jidongyan as he returns to his hometown.
A single separation from the mountain cave; years and months have passed in depth. The spring breeze remains in disarray even until now. Turning my head, the path before the crag is as it was before;
the hundred birds carrying flowers have nowhere to be found.
Seeing off Master Bing (who once requested instruction):
Counting the ink as he walks about does not cure hunger. Coming from the south, he has caught hold of a mere fragment.
People know of his former skills; let it be that these few people do not know him.
Seeing Master Jue off as he returns to Huazang Dun’an:
The expanse of his mind is as vast as Lake Tai; though the mountains lie low and the whirlwind roars, the waters do not surge.
A veteran hand who has long mastered the currents of the water, he must surely observe both the water itself and its ripples.
Seeing Master Ming off as he returns to Dongting:
Having cut across the current, he follows it again. The seventy-two peaks nod their heads in defiance.
Pressed to the point where there is not even a needle or a table, the vast expanse of Lake Tai spans three prefectures.

Sent forth to realize the True Dharma through non-attainment, (having returned from the imperial decree at the Huayan Pavilion), the misty waters of a hundred cities stretch boundlessly. A single staff traveled south and then flew north;
the gates of the pavilion opened on that very day, and even now not a hair’s breadth has shifted.
Master Shizhao demonstrates that illumination and function are simultaneous, merging them into a single platter. Yet the patch-robed monk opens his eyes and is deceived by him.
How does this compare to the constant samādhi of daily life, where the myriad phenomena stand in solemn stillness against their shadows?
To the Venerable Shijian:
Long laughter at Yunmen’s “Look and Yee!”—he instead draws out the character *gu* (look) and adds earth and mud to it.
Though a sword cast from the void leaves no trace, one will see the very void itself perish.
In my solitary hermitage, looking out in all four directions, all is vast and silent; I do not deceive myself. White clouds and flowing water drift east and west of their own accord.
Countless people travel the same path and follow the same tracks, yet they are all lost like birds that chase after blossoms.

Releasing the pond, all currents are cut off; from the very beginning, there is only stillness. Treading upon the single aperture, it flows forth in abundance. Do not debate whether one has reached the source or not;
even the Buddha does not know its lofty origin.
The six dissolve and the one perishes;
the six functions become useless as faith no longer penetrates. All at once it is entrusted to the spring breeze. A single curl of incense smoke lingers idly through the clear day;
though the hundred birds do not come, the flowers bloom red on their own.
Drawing lots to select the Thousand-Handed Avalokiteśvara:
autumn clears the myriad waters, the moon is in every house; spring enters the thousand forests, flowers are everywhere. I ask of the thousand hands and eyes of Great Compassion:
one does not know upon whose family the bright moon has fallen.
Addressing the Assembly (2):
Master Yeyi’s speech was laced with errors. "To achieve Buddhahood in early life and become a demon in old age; from head to toe, there is not a single bone of spiritual efficacy.
Yet how can you, in your admiration of his style, part the weeds to seek him?"
As soon as we met, he requested the *Chanyao*. Lately, there have been many spurious copies circulating in various quarters;
the manuscript of the *Huiriyao* is not of two different kinds, yet it is over a few minor points that the great confusion arises.
The lacquerer seeks a verse:
The lacquer bucket is naturally distinct; Do not labor to refine its excellence. Let it break into a hundred fragments; This will surely bring a moment of sorrow.
The attendant Bian, offering a tooth-relic of a Pratyekabuddha, requests ordination.
Mistakenly perceiving dependent origination, they remain unaware; the fallen sprout now belongs to the novice Bian.
If you wish to restore the ancestral Bian’s numinous bones, choose a monk who has achieved perfection—do not emulate him.

After writing these words of the Perfect Dharma, a fire-star flew from the heavens of the Third Dhyāna. Mountains, rivers, and the great earth were left without a single remnant. Who can comprehend this "broken-bottom" *huatou*?
A small iron spine remains to stabilize the realm of Kun-wei.
The stubbornness of Tian Tong Mizang is such that his calculations and deliberations have not yet triggered the kōan.
Amidst the wind and dust, at the slightest movement of grass, he harbors a hundred doubts. With his four corners collapsed to the ground, he is ashamed of his former deeds;
even if the void were to crumble, one would still listen to him.
It is shown that one must become like a person atop a rock;
one must first prepare a body as solid as stone. When the single thread is opened, even stone cannot compare. One must nod for oneself and grant approval within;
to wait for another’s approval is a waste of effort.
Master Fang is ascending Mount Jiangshan while also sending his greetings to Chijue, Wanshi, and Bichu.
Having already gone astray by seeking out various quarters, he now comes to join us to "beat the father's town. Now he is entering Zhongfu once more;
from error to error, there is no time of recovery. Those who wish to deliberate with him about these two errors will find that there is only the recognition of one’s own fault, and nothing else.
Kennon! You foolish old man, you stubborn elder—this was but an old dream shared between us. You know that from the beginning I have had no nostrils.
This is the "Portrait of Leaving the Mountains."
Casting aside the golden wheel as if it were but a trifle, he sat in deluded meditation for six years amidst the azure, rugged peaks.
Having failed to resolve even a small matter upon leaving the mountains, how could this compare to simply not entering them in the first place?
When the Great Being, ever contemplating (12),
gazes with fixed eyes and observes intently, the myriad threads of wind and sound, the roar of waves and snow, strike directly into right contemplation.
The sea mist clears; the mountain’s visage unfolds. A divine pearl rests in the palm; a bright mirror stands upon the dais. The Universal Gate is without lock or key;
worldly guests have never come.

When sounds form patterns, they are called "tones. Contemplating in this manner is like searching for a needle at the bottom of the sea. From the time of the King of Emptiness until now, my heart has drifted on.
In choosing the "Perfect Penetration" by joining the ranks, you needlessly took your stand in the wind. At that time, you made a confession of death, falsely claiming it was within hearing.
With a hundred and eight beads on his rosary, he counted from the beginning, keeping his mindfulness focused on each bead until he lost track of the number.
He thought to himself that it had been since the very first moment of hearing that he had entered the stream and lost the objective realm—though how many "donkey years" had passed, he could not say.
Potalaka Moon. A brushstroke from Longmen. The brush has its traces, but the moon leaves no tracks. To track its tracks, the Universal Gate (Pu-men) is utterly still.
Once the tracks are forgotten, the four directions are vast and majestic. (Behold the image of the moon.)
Sound is observed; form is also observed. After the kalpa of emptiness, before the kalpa of emptiness: wind stirs and dust rises; mountains are deep and waters are cold.
Ten thousand apertures are not stirred by wind; a thousand waves do not surge. The heavens are low, the moon is high; mountains are deep and waters are cold. The Universal Gate has no path to enter;
from beginning to end, it has never been locked.
From hearing, contemplation, and cultivation, one has gone astray; taking error for truth, one follows the current into the flow.
In the ghost cave of Mount Potalaka, there is but a half-moon of sea-silver in autumn.
Through hearing, contemplation, and cultivation, one enters samādhi; the two characteristics of movement and stillness clearly do not arise.
On Mount Potalaka, atop the White Flower Peak, one does not hear even a single cry from a warbling oriole.
A basket holds fish, not water; he does not eat them himself. Carrying it into the market, the scale has no markings, yet there is bait on the hook (the image of one carrying a fish basket).

For those who are distracted, such signs appear; yet when they are in meditative concentration, who is there to produce these images? When concentration and distraction are one and the same, these images are likewise non-existent.
If one says there are no images, it would be as vast a gulf as that between heaven and earth.
The Cloth Bag (6): Barefoot, he has just entered the marketplace;
turning his head, he laughs at people. What object is in his hand? He plays with an object whose name he does not know.
With eyes closed, he dozes; with eyes open, it is the consciousness of karma (*karmavijñāna*). To go on just like this—why such a frantic rush toward death?
Behind his back, he once opened the eyes of a ghost; though he has eyes, they lack sinews.
When asked about the affairs within the Tuṣita Heaven, he picked up a dried fish and held it up for others to see.
Laughing, he shatters the ancient sounds; turning his head, he is entirely pitiable. Now there is nothing more to laugh at; looking up, he laughs at the blue sky.
Barefoot one knows the sun; wearing clogs one knows the rain. As for this single point alone, I do not yet dare grant my approval.
Holding up dried fish, he strides through the long street; he says it was brought from the Celestial Palace. Iron—Fenghua’s people are as stubborn as iron.
When the Master has finished his laugh, who else is left to laugh?
In the continuity of the True [Dharma], there is no name; among the sages who have dispersed, there is no rank. Neither the Qin nor the Han can contain it—how shameful, how shameful!

There is nothing above in heaven and nothing below in earth; this very state of "nothingness" already obscures all things. To laboriously turn back one's head again only results in further entanglement and complication.
Vimalakīrti, in his inquiry after illness, flaunts his glib and overflowing tongue. Who is Mañjuśrī? He has never spoken of non-duality; he has already fallen into conceptual thought. Subhūti!
Having washed his feet, he sat cross-legged. Suddenly he exclaimed, "How rare! World-Honored One, what did you see at that time?
Hanshan pointed to the finger; Shigede grasped the finger and never saw the moon. It is like a short man watching a play.

Wearing robes of grass, his hair was matted like grass; before he had descended from Mount Wutai, a hundred strange omens appeared together, and the meaning of the sutra in his hand remained unresolved.
Let me ask you this for a moment: "Three times three in front, three times three behind"—how many is that?
If a young bride recites the Lotus Sutra, she shall marry him; empty flowers without stems—whom would they deceive? On the sands of the Jinshe River, there is golden sand.
Locked away. How long has this spring wind been left in such disarray?
Nü Lingzhao sets her wits against her father within the house; at the gate, she folds her sleeves to face Danxia. What a fine son, born of father and mother!
Daughter, there are those who have acquired so much useless clamor that they wear through their patched robes;
with needles too short and thread difficult to pass, they idly pick at them while basking in the sun. Do not disdain what is tattered; when you lift it up, it is complete in itself.

Having finished reading the remaining sutras, he began counting black beans from morning until after dusk. Seeing that the moon was like a crescent eyebrow, he suddenly realized the penetration of the divine rhinoceros horn. Thus it was with the First Patriarch.
The five petals of fragrance unfold from a single flower; no one has yet mapped its vines or pruned its roots and sprouts.
Had he not been forced to set foot upon the soil of Jinling, I would still regret that Xiao Liang had not yet become a master of his craft.
In praise of Master Chijue, this is an image of the First Patriarch Bodhidharma and Great Master Mazu.

His ears are pierced, yet they have never been bored through; his teeth are missing, yet they have never been broken. He crossed northward on a single reed raft; he returned west with only his sandals in hand.
Some call him the "stabilizing pillar in the middle of the stream" prior to the empty kalpa; others call him the one who "picked up the flower."

From this point forward, whether it be "the golden mouth and wooden tongue," or what some call "the orthodox tradition versus the divergent tunes," or again "direct pointing versus circuitous explanations"—none of these are what I call the Way.
As for those who seek the vessel of the Mahāyāna, they travel a hundred thousand li, waiting for someone to inspire them.
How could his capacity not be that of the Mahāyāna? From youth he bore the burden of prior awakening; according to the rites, he came as a student to learn, and having learned, he realized it.
Since these four qualities are so distant and profound, and he bears them all, I fear that even the iron of the Five Indias would be insufficient to cast this error.
The Golden Cock’s poison: a single grain of millet has not yet trodden upon a person to kill them, yet their feet have already stumbled.
At the eighteen rapids, the dead waters were dammed and turned back; of the eighty-four men, none perished in the submersion.
At Hongdu, at Letan, the ancestral wind blew with unrestrained ferocity. One wave stirs and ten thousand waves arise; branching and subdividing, such is the current everywhere. Furthermore—
Not a single person recognizes the profound principle; there is only Gui-zong who is slightly more capable. Upon careful examination, this is the very bottom line spoken by Xuansha and Puhua.
The wind-driven madness has been exhausted until nothing remains. A single coffin carried by eight men; they carry it out beyond the walls of Zhenzhou City.

East, south, west, north—the gates open on both sides. We have met; ten thousand eight thousand miles away.

Linji was a thief who steals in broad daylight. This fellow strips off the ghost’s turban and assumes my robes and colors; he stands there with his gourd-pot and immediately intends to sink it, yet he will not let the iron weight fall into the well and drown.

Regarding the essential teaching of Huangbo: it seems Huangbo had nowhere to clear his grievance.

When Yangqi (Yan Xuechao requested [the teaching] using three items—a three-legged donkey, a vajra-ring, and a jujube thorn—claiming these constituted a violation of the prohibitions)—he invited Ciming for an evening discourse.
Upon seeing the "White Snow," he laughed heartily, saying, "To act as a father and yet not be compassionate; to act as a son and yet not be filial. Such a person..."
In the affairs of commerce and concealment, I dare to call myself one who tends the grass for the blind donkey. I do not wonder that people say I do not understand Chan;
a smoothing-iron brews tea, which is no different from a cauldron.

To rejoice, he sleeps; to scold, he sleeps; when awake, he sleeps; when weary, he sleeps. Son of good family, arise! Such is the nature of phenomena (dharmatā).

The Eight-Lara-Zha of Dongshan’s shelf—only a gentleman can handle it. Aconite and the same hometown are equally pungent; chewing through a lump of fermented sour dough is like biting into a mass of iron.

Yet, with a single flick of his mechanism, Wuyue knitted his brows; his skill was exhausted. He then cast down his bamboo staff.

The Great Master Zhi was seated before a precious desk, the *cintāmaṇi* in his hand. With shoulders like those of Yu and eyes like those of Tang, with eyes like the Yellow River and a mouth like the sea, he found his holy teacher amidst the mountains of Mount Nanyue.

Before the mountain had even dispersed,

I regret that I died under the National Teacher’s phrase. A dead eye opens to life; not a single thread remains hanging.

like a phoenix crossing a hearth amidst the snow, he shattered all bonds. There were no longer two of them. His reputation spread across the lakes and seas as he traveled to give formal sermons, and all vied to admire his solitary wind.

The tip of the ladle emerges from the bottom; like a phoenix, like a qilin. When the head of the board is raised and stirred, it covers heaven and earth without revealing a single sharp edge—this is a true man.
This is still the matter that the Head Seat Sheng and all quarters have in common.
But as for the news where ten thousand mountains are buried under snow and the white ox leaves no tracks—who knows it thoroughly? It does not hinder the fire.

Like the abbot who entered the stupa, a monk of peace under the Five Dynasties’ emperors, he is not entangled in the dead vines of various quarters. North of the Tán and south of the Xiāng, he stands tall and solitary.
Falling. He has long burned the lamp within the seamless stupa.

taking it up, one encounters its source at every turn. The dream of a hundred years is shattered, suddenly like a cicada shedding its shell.

in this great peace, the old man holds his torch.

within the lion’s roar, the hearts of foxes, wolves, and jackals all fail. In a single vessel, mosquitoes and gnats buzz and chirp;
atop the seat, an owl hoots from time to time. A spider weaves its web in the corner of the bed; he calls this "catching dragons and striking phoenixes. Upon reaching—

A procession of plain cotton shirts, unstained by the defilements of the three paths. With a single stroke of brilliance, they are ten times more refined and elegant.
Wild fires spontaneously consume the heavens; they cast off their mother-born trousers.

His disciple sent a letter saying: "Our late teacher lived for seventy-one years and spent over thirty summers in full ordination.

His resolve was to transform and guide those of his region, leading them toward goodness. It is further said: "Though he did not engage in Zen meditation nor study the teachings, in all that he did, he dared not abandon himself.
This is what is meant by the saying: "Xuansha did not cross the ridge; Baoshou did not ford the river;
without spending a single coin, he purchased the entire splendor. It is also said: "In my later years, I fashioned a Buddha."
He provided meals for the Sangha, closed his door to the world, and swept away all distractions to focus single-mindedly on practice. This was precisely what Xuefeng meant when he said:

"Do not fail to raise others' faults repeatedly, but you should eliminate your own transgressions gradually. Finally, he remarked: "The shadow of lightning does not linger; recite the Buddha's name with utmost sincerity.
Shave your hair and wash your body, then pass away in serene stillness. Thus, it was as the sutras describe: he had foreknowledge seven days in advance.
Knowing for himself that the time had come, at the moment of full clarity, he was as if entering meditative absorption; one could say he had reached the limit of birth and death.
This was how his life’s karmic connections were formed within the temple of the Butcher Grand Guardian, and how they were brought to fruition.
Yet, even so, Shishuang said: "To go to the incense burner in an ancient temple"—how can this be explained? It must be such that it reaches through the three periods of time.
The Buddhas could not speak of it; the six generations of patriarchs could not lift it up; the old monks of the world have no way to peer into it.
How then could I know it or speak of it? (Holding up a torch, he says: Stop your ears and listen to this speaking!
Chan Shouzuo held the torch for his own death after traveling on pilgrimage to Zhaozhou; he was born from the time before the black bean had sprouted.
Entering birth and exiting death, there is nothing else—yet who is it that is ultimately unborn? Do you wish to see this Chan Shouzuo who is unborn? He has wandered throughout all of heaven.
The Boundary. The Sun of Wisdom, in his final years, uses gentleness to subdue the harsh; its application is perfectly timed. At times he rejoices:
the coral forest trees are bathed in the brilliant light of the sun. At times he is incensed: he shakes the great city of the triple world, transforming cool serenity into feverish affliction.

When the world perishes, he does not decay. [To you,] O person: before the Stūpa of Many Sons, there is no need to turn back your head.
Supporting Master Zishang’s Entry into the Stupa (during the time of Xiuyan in the assembly at Yuyang; at that time, Fozhao resided at Dong’an).
He was poor and possessed no surplus belongings. Having long possessed the bones of a sage, he had been forged and refined within a great furnace and emerged from a heap of dead ashes.
He cannot be hidden away; he bows high to Śākyamuni but does not prostrate to Maitreya. There is absolutely no rank or position to be arranged;
turning his body, he plunges straight down into the dragon’s cave.

he was clear in bestowing rewards and meting out punishments, and he destroyed prohibitions and regulations, overturning the established path. He possessed the backbone of cast iron; entering fire, he would not be burned.

Tai: Turning over and going thus—going thus, all doubt and conjecture are cut off. The yellow leaves fall in the wind;
white dew dots the gray moss.

is this the same as or different from the "Manifest Knowledge and Tolerance" of the Four Directions? If you say they are the same, you are catching the wind; if you say they are different, you are grasping at the moon.
If they were the same, they would be the same from beginning to end; if they were different, they would be different from beginning to end. Guest Official Jing, tread upon and sever the river!

The Eighteen Rapids of the West. From teaching that "water burns beneath the earth and fire blazes in the heavens," the true West Hall Master took up his torch and passed away while sitting, vanishing like a somersault from the back.
He was a wild rogue atop the tower, yet he remained impaled in the mud. Although this constitutes two parts, it is one whole.
They are not the same. To simply transcend through a single gate is still my Pure Land. This is the place where a true Chan master ordinarily walks and dwells.

As for shifting positions and returning the faculty, or acting secretly and employing mysteries—this does not belong to the time before Dīpaṃkara, nor does it fall within the period after the empty kalpa.
The spring wind dances wildly among the willows by the embankment; listen now to the lion’s roar from amidst the flames.

"Where are the three rivers and nine embankments? The dream of the ancient cypress and three crags has already faded. These are all places where we once walked;

yet now there is only worry that wind and rain will make it difficult to cross the river. Whether the wind is cold or the rain is cold, it matters not at all. A spark of stone-fire, a flash of lightning.

the Great Master Tōng took leave of his kin and severed his attachments to go forth as a nun. Perhaps Bānqiān [will] follow from the beginning.

present pearls, following the promptness of the Dragon Girl Sagara. Of those who live a hundred years, seventy is rare. Nevertheless, once dead, one is burned.
There is still this tiny star; it is this very star that even the Buddha-eye can hardly perceive. Within the seamless stupa, its entirety is fully manifested;
with a single turn of the body, the five Sumeru mountains are toppled.

the ten directions are clear and vast, refusing to be obscured by superficial coatings. Within the dense array of the myriad phenomena, not even a shadow or substance can escape.

Utterly free from the gaps and leaks of the scaffolding, his practice is subtle and precise, and his strategic insight is brilliant.

He intends to emulate the thousand-year-old Master who dwelt in the mountains, yet he laughs at Zhaozhou’s eighty years of wandering. Amidst celestial incense and auspicious snow, he makes a small trial of the total upholding;

yet of the clouds, moon, streams, and mountains, he possesses but half. With the tripod of the three powers once more set upon the head of the matter—though the "head of the matter" is indeed present—for now, let us consider this.

It is said that Mañjuśrī spent the summer retreats in three places, dividing the tripod with Ding—were they the same or different? Throughout the vast world of the various quarters, who can discern this?
Entrust it to the broad and long tongue of the sound of the mountain stream.

Draw water. With one hand, set fire to it.

As for the "Qian" (乾) attendant initiating the materials, it is as set forth in the *Hongfan*: among the five blessings of Jizi, if there were no virtuous people, how could they be fulfilled? The first is longevity. Seven.

your granaries will be filled and your stores piled high, like mountain ridges and hills. Third is health and tranquility. Your face shall never wrinkle; when sleeping, you close your eyes; when eating, you open your mouth.
Fourth is the pursuit of virtue. Take the worthy as your model; follow those who are advanced in wisdom.

Make offerings to the Tathāgata throughout the ocean of three thousand lands across the Bhadrakalpa. Examining daily life, rely on the "Song of the Twelve Hours" by the Ancients.
